column3: It repeats the interrogative "what prevented you," but concerns Iblis's refusal to prostrate rather than a guardian's response to communal deviation.
Its fear-and-reliance scene offers only a distant contrast to Harun's stated concern for communal cohesion.
It portrays an effort to lead others astray, clarifying the kind of collective deviation Musa says Harun witnessed.
It closely shares the question about what prevented obedience, though Iblis's refusal differs from Harun's restrained intervention.
It gives the people's explicit persistence in worshipping the calf until Musa returns, the deviation Harun had to confront.
The elite falsely call Nuh misguided, a reversed accusation that only broadly parallels the focus's judgment of deviation.
Its conditional seeing describes the appearance of immortal youths, not recognizing moral deviation.
Harun directly explains that he feared dividing Israel and failing Musa's instruction, answering the question posed in the focus.
It depicts mockers labeling believers misguided, the inverse of Musa's justified recognition of his people's error.
Yusuf's dream-vision has no material relation to seeing communal deviation or intervening in it.
It is the parallel account of Musa angrily confronting Harun after the calf episode and supplies Harun's fuller account of the constraint.
Its description of one who withholds good does not explain Harun's restraint before Israel's idolatry.
A prophet's call for God-consciousness is a broad corrective to error but adds no specific relation to Harun's dilemma.
The next ayah sharpens Musa's charge: Harun did not follow him and appeared to disobey his command.
Unseen divine support in battle does not clarify the confrontation over the calf.
Misleading outward appearance and speech offer a remote contrast to Harun's observation of an openly visible deviation.
The sinners' humbled posture and belated confession do not bear on Harun's responsibility to act.
It distinguishes a truthful inner perception from what was seen, but does not address a leader's response to observed error.
Its fearful hypocrites are ungenerous and verbally harsh, not a community Harun must correct for idolatry.
It identifies the calf as unable to answer, harm, or benefit, establishing the manifest irrationality of the deviation Musa mentions.
The brothers wrongly call their father misguided; the reversed accusation gives little help with Musa's actual judgment of Israel.
It names a belief-obstacle to accepting guidance, but not the restraint of one who has already recognized deviation.
The warning to those who fear the Hour only broadly resembles a prophet's warning of an erring people.
Seeing the earth turn green does not clarify moral recognition or intervention.
The confession that false gods vanished is a distant consequence of idolatry, not Harun's contemporaneous response.
It records Harun's prior warning, command to follow him, and appeal to obey, showing that he had already intervened verbally.
Its unavailable and unwithheld provision is unrelated to the obstacle in Musa's question.
Blocking others from God's path and being far astray broadly relates to misguidance but not to the focus scene.
The weighty revelation relates only remotely to the entrusted command Harun was expected to observe.
The Prophet's vision of great signs does not illuminate Harun's observation of Israel's error.
The loss of false objects of worship recalls idolatry's failure but does not clarify the calf episode's response.
Withholding small assistance is a different sense of prevention and offers no useful account of Harun's constraint.
Seeing the smallest evil deed at judgment is not relevant to recognizing and confronting communal deviation.
Ibrahim's question about worship is a broad anti-idolatry challenge, less specific than the calf material already present.
The night prayer's more upright speech does not clarify Musa and Harun's exchange.
The stated reason for withholding signs is a distinct divine prevention, not Harun's human restraint.
It names what prevents people from believing and seeking forgiveness, only lexically resembling Musa's question.
Self-restraint from desire is a different ethical restraint from Harun's fear of splitting the people.
Disputing and hastening the Hour does not bear on the calf episode.
Israel later realizes that it went astray after making the calf, directly confirming the deviation Musa says Harun saw.
Taking God as trustee does not clarify the disputed intervention.
A second visionary sight is unrelated to the focus's recognition of deviation.
It describes people who went astray through uninformed religious judgments, a broad analogue to Israel's false worship.
Failure to urge feeding the poor has no focused relation to Harun's restraint.
Seeing the promised punishment approach does not clarify the focus scene.
A people prohibiting Lut from receiving others is a different form of interference, not a response to observed deviation.
The companions of the right have no bearing on Musa's question.
The absence of sun and cold in Paradise is unrelated.
The exchange about a missing measure does not clarify the focus.
Expecting one's reckoning is unrelated to Harun's conduct.
Musa identifies a violent partisan act as satanic and misleading, only generally relevant to resisting misguidance.
Ibrahim's invitation to eat has no relation to the focus.
Preventing God's name from being mentioned is an unrelated obstruction, not Harun's reason for restraint.
Shuayb's call to fear God is a generic prophetic warning with little added value here.
It reverses an accusation of great misguidance onto those who rejected a warning, a distant rhetorical parallel.
Iblis being reprieved does not clarify Musa's question.
It explains why hypocrites' acts are not accepted, a different kind of internal obstacle.
Ibrahim's rebuke of idol worship broadly parallels confronting false worship, but lacks the focus's leadership dilemma.
Following desire without knowledge produces misguidance, a general background to the people's error.
Iblis being reprieved does not relate to the focus.
It says Pharaoh led his people astray, a nearby contrast in which a leader causes rather than attempts to stop communal misguidance.
One brother's prior reminder to his companions is only a loose parallel to Harun's warning.
It describes those who stray from God's path, but does not explain a witness's duty or constraint.
Iblis being reprieved has no focused connection.
It distinguishes personal right guidance from others' deviation, but does not resolve a leader's communal responsibility.
Musa's designation of Harun as his brother supplies the relationship underlying the charged exchange, though it adds little about the episode.
A final confession of manifest error is a distant consequence of misguidance.
It announces that the Samiri led Musa's people astray during his absence, directly setting up the deviation at issue.
It calls idol worship manifest error, a broad theological parallel to the calf worship.
The question whether idols hear worshippers is a general critique of idolatry, less direct than 20:89.
Israel's demand to see God is another failure of the same community but does not clarify Harun's constrained action.
Yusuf confronts his brothers over their past wrongdoing, only loosely resembling Musa's reproach of Harun.
God's hearing and seeing in Musa and Harun's mission echoes perception language but does not address the calf dispute.
The garden owners initially mistake what they see, contrasting only distantly with Harun correctly recognizing deviation.
The rupture between leaders and followers at judgment broadly contrasts with Harun's effort to avoid dividing Israel.
God restraining Israel from harming Isa is a different protective intervention and does not explain Harun's choice.
The chiefs' social judgment of Nuh and his followers is unrelated to the focus's actual deviation.
Ibrahim challenges his father for worshipping what cannot hear or see, a broad anti-idolatry parallel.
Guidance during pilgrimage does not clarify the calf episode.
Ibrahim confronts his people over their idols and their devotion to them, a meaningful but general parallel to Israel's calf worship.
Inherited adherence to astray ancestors broadly parallels a community persisting in error.
The inquiry into Yusuf's affair is unrelated to the focus.
The Prophet's looking heavenward and change of direction only remotely echoes the focus's seeing and guidance language.
The withholding of grain is a different use of prevention and adds no clarity to Harun's restraint.
Musa describes a past act committed while astray, offering a personal example of misguidance without the communal-response issue.
Seeking judgment from false authority illustrates choosing a misleading authority, broadly analogous to turning toward the calf.
Exchanging guidance for error concerns misguidance generally but adds nothing to Harun's action.
Lut confronts his people over a grave wrong, a generic prophetic rebuke rather than the focus's question about restraint.
It attributes people's misguidance to criminals, only broadly related to the Samiri's leading of Israel astray.
Ibrahim says he sees his father and people in manifest error because of idols, closely paralleling recognition of communal idolatry.
The man urges his people to follow the messengers, a general call to guidance with little added detail.
Calling despair a mark of the astray is unrelated to the calf episode's intervention.
The command to leave those who deviate regarding God's names does not clarify Harun's situation.
Being most astray in path is a general final judgment, not the observed deviation in the focus.
Shuayb's warning to his people is a generic example of prophetic correction.
Misleading comparisons that make opponents stray do not illuminate the focus's leadership conflict.
Internal dispute and disobedience after seeing what was desired show a community fracturing under failed obedience, relevant to Harun's fear of division.
A person's withholding when touched by good is an unrelated sense of restraint.
Idolaters excuse worship by appealing to God's will, a distant rationalization for false worship.
It denies that the Prophet is astray, only a general contrast to the focus's stated misguidance.
Musa explicitly appoints Harun as his deputy, commands him to set matters right, and warns him not to follow corrupters, forming the governing instruction behind Musa's question.
It narrates Israel's taking of the speaking-less calf during Musa's absence, the exact deviation Harun saw.
Immediately after the parallel confrontation, Musa includes Harun in his prayer for forgiveness and mercy, showing the dispute's fraternal resolution.
It states the wrath and humiliation awaiting those who took the calf, supplying the consequence of the deviation at issue.
It supplies the restorative outcome for those who committed evil, then repented and believed, following the calf transgression.
God asks Musa what made him hasten ahead of his people, introducing the separation that left Harun with the community.
Musa says his people are following behind him and that he hastened to please God, directly explaining the circumstances of Harun's temporary charge.
Musa returns to his people angry and grieving and rebukes their breach during his absence, immediately leading into his question to Harun.
The people explain that they were made to bear and then cast the Egyptians' ornaments, giving their own account of how they entered the calf episode.
It identifies the object made for them as the calf and records their false claim that it was their god and Musa's god.
Musa turns from Harun to question the Samiri, identifying the separate instigator of the people's deviation.
The Samiri explains his act of casting what he had grasped, providing his account of the mechanism behind the calf's production.
Musa condemns and banishes the Samiri and declares the calf will be destroyed, completing the corrective action absent during Harun's restraint.
It closes the episode by affirming that God alone is the deity, directly overturning the people's calf worship.
It recalls that Israel took the calf after Musa's appointed absence, a concise retrospective statement of the event.
Musa tells his people they wronged themselves by taking the calf and commands their repentance, directly framing the error Harun had tried to arrest.
It states that Israel took the calf after Musa brought clear proofs, reinforcing the culpability of their deviation.
It links the covenant with Israel's declaration of disobedience and the calf's absorption into their hearts, clarifying the community's entrenched refusal.
It recalls that Israel took the calf after clear proofs and that God nevertheless pardoned them, a later summary of the same transgression.
